summary: The narrator, visiting an adoption-related appointment, reviews country-specific adoption organizations that handle orphans from Russia, Ecuador and Brazil, noting their slow processes and asking about a fast track for a healthy baby. Accompanied by Lou, who is on a better-than-usual morning, the narrator drives up the Hudson to Quetzal Manor, a former Carmelite convent that looks like a Gothic, imposing building. The narrator is still recovering from a cold, and the passage sets up a meeting with someone who seems to know more about the narrator than vice versa.
one_line: The narrator and Lou drive to the imposing former convent Quetzal Manor for an unusual appointment while seeking a fast-track baby adoption.
key_facts: Cradle of Hope specialized in orphaned Russian kids.
Children and Families, Inc., provided adoptions for Equadorian children.
International Adoption Assistance, Inc., handled Brazilian orphans.
The narrator asked whether there was some kind of new fast track for a brand-new healthy baby in just a few months, and the question was always taken as a joke.

The narrator convinced Lou to come along partly for the security of having him present after a threatening phone call to Paula and a Hispanic thug who accosted the narrator outside her apartment building.
The narrator wished Steve could materialize and be with them, but Steve was absent.
The drive went up Riverside Drive, then the Henry Hudson Parkway, with a flawless blue sky and the wide Hudson river.
Lou had noticeably less of a hangover than usual, and was in elevated spirits over Sarah's momentary brush with consciousness.
After crossing the Henry Hudson Bridge, the group left the highway and followed a service road toward the river.
Quetzal Manor had an imposing open gate and a tree-shrouded driveway.
Carly had told the narrator that Quetzal Manor had once been a Carmelite convent dating from the middle of the last century.
The building featured endless arches of cut stone, turrets, and gargoyles, and was described as a monument to Church authority.
The narrator described the house as truly magisterial yet more than a little creepy, like a brooding homage to medieval torture.
The car parked under a huge oak tree in front of the building.
The narrator had a cold that still lingered and made their mind feel less than fully working.
